input: Lobby my HOA to add a community garden plot

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Knowing whether the user wants a single personal plot or a multi-resident shared garden changes the scale of the proposal, the land required, and the complexity of the ask.
Whether the user is lobbying alone or has neighbors already on board determines whether the first step is building support internally or going straight to the HOA board.
The current HOA stance — whether they have rules that explicitly forbid gardens, are silent on the topic, or have shown prior interest — fundamentally shapes the strategy and tone needed.
There may be a specific HOA meeting deadline, an upcoming vote, or a submission window that determines how quickly the plan must come together.
Knowing what land or space is actually available (unused common area, a specific lot, rooftop, etc.) determines whether a site proposal can be included from the start.
The user may want a formal written proposal, a petition drive, a presentation at a meeting, or a casual conversation first — their preferred approach shapes the entire plan.
The user's definition of success matters — a formal HOA vote to approve, a pilot program, a dedicated budget line, or simply getting the idea on the agenda are very different endpoints.

gold.taskTitle: Lobby HOA to approve a community garden plot
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to persuade their HOA to establish a community garden plot in their neighborhood.

questions.title: How many plots — just yours, or a shared multi-resident garden?
questions.description: Clarify whether this is a proposal for a single personal garden plot or a larger shared community garden with multiple participating residents.

questions.title: Do you have neighbors who already support this idea?
questions.description: Determine whether the user has allies among residents, which affects whether the immediate next step is coalition-building or going directly to the HOA board.

questions.title: What is the HOA's current stance on gardens or landscaping changes?
questions.description: Find out if the HOA has rules that explicitly prohibit gardens, is silent on the topic, or has previously shown openness — this determines the strategy and tone of the pitch.

questions.title: Is there a specific HOA meeting or submission deadline coming up?
questions.description: Identify any hard time constraints such as an upcoming board meeting, annual vote, or proposal submission window that would set the pace of the lobbying effort.

questions.title: Is there a specific piece of land or common area you have in mind?
questions.description: Determine whether the user has already identified a candidate location, which affects whether a concrete site proposal can be included in the pitch from the start.

questions.title: How do you want to make your case — written proposal, petition, or presentation?
questions.description: Understand the user's preferred approach to lobbying so the plan can be built around the right format and communication style.

questions.title: What does a win look like — a formal vote, a pilot program, or something else?
questions.description: Define the user's success criteria so the plan targets the right outcome, whether that is a binding HOA resolution, a small trial plot, a budget allocation, or simply getting on the agenda.
